transcript_body:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-21
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Aaron Patel (Redwood AE), Samira Gomez (Redwood SE), Emily Chen (CTO - Cedar), Rajiv Kumar (Head of SecOps - Cedar), Lindsey Park (Platform Eng - Cedar), Maya Ortiz (Legal - Cedar)
Artifacts referenced: private-vpc-arch-v1.pdf (Redwood), SOC2-summary-2025.pdf (Redwood link), redwood-private-terraform.zip (sample), cedar-compliance-questions.xlsx (customer)

[00:00] Aaron (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick intros?
[00:08] Emily (Cedar): emily here, cto at cedar, i'll be high level, rajiv is our secops lead, lindsey does the platform work, maya is with legal for compliance Qs.
[00:16] Aaron: perfect, samira is our solutions engineer, she'll run through the private vpc topology and answer network questions. goal is to validate we can meet your egress/ingress constraints and key management needs.
[00:28] Samira (Redwood SE): hi all; i'll share my screen in a sec. one note — apologies if redwood product names get mashed, my mic is a little echo-y.
[00:35] [screen share starts: private-vpc-arch-v1.pdf]
[00:40] Samira: ok the high level is we run a private control plane that sits in your VPC under a customer-managed subnet. all inference nodes are in private subnets behind no public IPs; control plane comms go over a dedicated endpoint (we can do VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink). ingress for your app traffic typically goes through an internal NLB or ALB depending on the protocol.
[01:05] Rajiv: can you confirm there are no outbound internet paths from the inference nodes by default? we need to restrict egress to our approved proxies only.
[01:12] Samira: yes by default nodes are in private subnets with no IGW; egress is handled via NAT gateway or a centralized egress proxy. we support routing through customer-managed gateway/firewall appliance. we also document patterns for deny-all and explicit allow lists.
[01:30] Lindsey: our concern is maintenance windows and package pulls for model updates. how do you handle updates without allowing open egress?
[01:38] Samira: two patterns — 1) use an internal artifact repo mirror reachable over private endpoints (we recommend pulling packages into your mirror) or 2) allow egress to a very small set of Redwood CDNs or signed S3 buckets; we can provide IP ranges and signed URLs. for security-conscious customers we do a signed artifact workflow so nothing is pulled from the public internet directly.
[01:55] Aaron: note — we'll attach the signed S3 workflow doc in the follow-up.
[02:02] Maya (Legal): on the KMS front, can you confirm customer-managed keys and HSM support? we have requirements to hold encryption keys in customer control for certain datasets.
[02:12] Samira: we support BYOK with customer-managed KMS keys. for cloud HSM-level protection we integrate with AWS CloudHSM or external HSM via KMIP in on-prem installations. envelope encryption is supported: data keys are encrypted with your CMK. we also keep control plane metadata separate from your customer data.
[02:33] Rajiv: what about key rotation and auditability? we need logs of every decrypt and key usage.
[02:40] Samira: KMS generates CloudTrail events for key usage; we surface decrypted operations in the audit log stream. we can forward audit logs to your S3 bucket or to a SIEM over our log-forwarder. retention and export are configurable — how long do you need to keep logs?
[02:58] Rajiv: current policy is 7 years for some artifacts, but for telemetry we usually keep 2 years. need to check specifics.
[03:06] Aaron: ok we'll note retention as an open item — cedar to confirm.
[03:12] [03:12] Topic switch: firewalling and network controls
[03:16] Samira: we usually recommend layered controls: security groups for instance-level port restrictions (allow only 443 between app layer and inference nodes), NACLs as subnet-level guardrails for accidental misconfig, and a central virtual firewall appliance (Palo Alto, Fortinet) or cloud-native firewall for deep packet inspection / IPS.
[03:36] Rajiv: if we use a firewall appliance, can traffic be hairpinned through it? latency impact ok?
[03:42] Samira: yes hairpinned egress is common; we try to keep the data path optimized. inference traffic is high-throughput — for latency-sensitive routes we recommend colocating the firewall in the same AZ and using high-bandwidth instances. we can also do inline eBPF-based filtering at the host level for smaller rulesets to avoid extra hops.
[04:05] Lindsey: about security groups — do you manage them or do we?
[04:09] Samira: customer-managed is the default for private deployments; we provide recommended templates (Terraform) and can operate them under an ops agreement. the terraform sample shows modules for subnets, route tables, SGs, and NACLs.
[04:24] [04:24] Topic: ingress and private endpoints
[04:27] Samira: ingress options — internal NLB + TLS termination in your vpc; alternatively we support AWS PrivateLink endpoints so your services call a VPC endpoint without traversing internet. PrivateLink reduces attack surface since there's no public DNS entry.
[04:43] Emily: PrivateLink sounds good but our networking team is picky about cross-account peering. what's easiest operationally?
[04:49] Aaron: PrivateLink tends to be simpler operationally for some customers — it's cross-account and controlled; VPC peering has route table management overhead. we'll detail tradeoffs in the follow-up doc.
[04:59] [05:00] Topic: audit logs and SIEM integration
[05:03] Samira: audit pipeline — control plane and inference logs can be forwarded to your S3 bucket encrypted with your KMS key, or we can push to your SIEM via TLS syslog/forwarder. logs include request metadata, model version, request hashes (we avoid storing PII by default unless you opt-in).
[05:24] Rajiv: is there any PII in the logs? we need to comply with data residency rules.
[05:29] Samira: by default we mask or hash payloads; payload retention is configurable. for regulated workloads we recommend redwood-private with on-prem or VPC-only egress and endpoint controls so data never leaves the region.
[05:45] Maya: speaking of residency, do you support region-specific deployment and controlled backups?
[05:50] Samira: yes, you can pin region and availability zones. backups (model caches, persistent storage) can be stored in your customer-managed buckets in-region. snapshot exports are encrypted with your CMK.
[06:03] [06:03] Topic: SSO, RBAC, provisioning
[06:06] Aaron: quick note on SSO — we support SAML SSO (Okta, Azure AD) and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is pluggable; roles map to API tokens and console roles.
[06:18] Lindsey: we already have Okta + SCIM; can you do automated provisioning and role sync?
[06:23] Samira: yes, we support SCIM sync for groups to roles; we can also integrate with your IDP for MFA enforcement policies.
[06:32] Rajiv: any integrations for audit of admin actions? we need to tie admin console actions to user identities.
[06:37] Samira: admin activities are logged and mapped to SAML identities; logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. we also support RBAC with fine-grained permissions for admin, read-only, and operator roles.
[06:49] [06:49] Topic: on-prem considerations and offline mode
[06:51] Samira: for air-gapped on-prem we package a private control plane image and provide installation guides. network interactions to Redwood remote services are minimized; key exchange and license attestation can be done via signed tokens or offline bundle. HSM integration is supported locally.
[07:12] Emily: our compliance team will likely prefer on-prem for certain regulated models; what's the expected ops overhead?
[07:18] Samira: higher ops overhead vs cloud but we provide scripts and terraform-like manifests for common infra. we can also offer a managed private option where Redwood manages the control plane inside your VPC under strict runbooks.
[07:33] [07:33] Rajiv: question — how do you guarantee graceful failure if the control plane loses connectivity? we need local inference to continue during control plane outages.
[07:40] Samira: inference nodes cache model weights and KV cache; they can continue serving with previous model until control plane is restored. we also support fallback policies to a local read-only mode. we'll document RTO/RPO expectations per SLA.
[07:56] [08:00] Brief silence / side chatter about calendar invites
[08:12] Lindsey: can you share recommended NACL rules and example security group that only allows 443 from our app subnets?
[08:19] Samira: yes — the terraform samples include that. we'll add a hardened SG example and a minimal NACL template.
[08:27] Aaron: circling back to KMS, maya had legal questions?
[08:30] Maya: just to confirm — do you provide evidence for key custody separation and access logs for audits? we need attestation for SOC2 auditors.
[08:38] Samira: yes the SOC2 summary shows key custody controls; access logs for key usage are retrievable via CloudTrail and we can produce exported event sets for audits. we'll include the SOC2 cert and the KMS controls page in the follow-up.
[08:52] [08:52] Topic: egress control patterns (detailed)
[08:55] Samira: patterns: 1) NAT Gateway with packet filtering and proxy, 2) Explicit PrivateLink to Redwood endpoints, 3) Hairpin via firewall appliance with IDS/IPS, 4) Air-gapped with manual sync. each has tradeoffs on latency, operational complexity, and security posture.
[09:15] Rajiv: do you have a minimal-latency pattern recommendation for synchronous low-latency requests?
[09:20] Samira: colocated private endpoints + internal NLB and minimal hairpin through the same AZ firewall; avoid cross-AZ hops. also use instance types with enhanced networking.
[09:31] [09:31] Topic: monitoring and observability
[09:33] Samira: we expose per-route latency and token-level metrics to the Redwood Console; for private deployments you can forward metrics to Prometheus/Grafana via pushgateway or pull from our metrics endpoint with mTLS.
[09:49] Lindsey: how are secrets stored on the host?
[09:52] Samira: secrets are stored encrypted on disk; we support secrets via the OS-level keyring and integration with the KMS for decrypt on boot. ephemeral keys for runtime memory are used.
[10:05] [10:05] Quick clarification and cross-talk about certificate rotation
[10:12] Aaron: we'll include cert rotation guidance; typical cadence is 90 days for leaf certs depending on your policy.
[10:20] Maya: one more legal ask — do you sign a data processing addendum and accept certain transfer restrictions?
[10:27] Aaron: yes we have standard DPA templates and can accept additional clauses; we'll route legal to legal after this.
[10:34] [10:34] Wrap up and next steps
[10:35] Aaron: recap — Redwood will send network diagram, terraform examples, SOC2 summary, and signed artifact workflow. cedar will send CIDR ranges, egress allowed list, and compliance questionnaire updates. we'll set a bench test for private deployment week of 8/26.
[10:50] Emily: thanks, this was helpful.
[10:53] Rajiv: thanks everyone.
[10:55] [call ends]

Notes on transcript: occasional mic overlaps, speaker labels approximate; some product names auto-transcribed differently in places.
